issues.title: [Software] HotaruNet: Protocol-adaptive anti-censorship client for Android & Windows (VLESS REALITY, WARP, Hysteria 2)
issues.body:
### Overview & Context
In environments with state-level Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) and dynamic throttling (such as Iranian telecoms including MCI, MTN Irancell, and fixed ADSL/VDSL, as well as similar censorship firewalls), simple network reachability tests (e.g., 0-byte HTTP 204 checks or TCP handshakes) regularly yield false positives: a node appears "connected", but sustained data transfer is throttled down to 0 KB/s.

To address this, we developed **HotaruNet** (latest release: **v2.3.44**), an open-source censorship-resistant client for Android and Windows 10/11 designed around empirical throughput probing and dynamic protocol adaptation.

### Core Architecture & Design Principles
1. **Empirical Throughput Probing (Speed & Bandwidth over Ping)**:
   - Rather than relying on ICMP or zero-byte 204 pings, Go-based JNI probes execute sequential calibrated download measurements (~32 KiB payloads over CDN assets / `speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=32768`).
   - Probe timeouts are tuned to 4000ms to allow cold TLS handshakes to complete without false-negative zero reports under latency jitter.
   - Candidate routing score is dominated by empirical download throughput (`Bps`) and the `throughput / latency` ratio.

2. **Protocol-Adaptive Auto-Selection**:
   - The engine dynamically monitors and switches between censorship-resistant transports:
     - **VLESS REALITY** (TCP 443 + Vision flow)
     - **Cloudflare WARP Dedicated** (WireGuard across clean Anycast IP ranges)
     - **Hysteria 2** (QUIC / UDP with custom BBR congestion control)
     - **XHTTP / SplitHTTP** (HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 transport)
     - **WebSocket + TLS** (reverse proxy / CDN fallback)

3. **Live Watchdog & Degradation Failover**:
   - Active background monitoring probes download throughput every 25–35 seconds.
   - If throughput drops below the streaming threshold (64 KB/s) for 3 consecutive intervals (`slowSamples >= 3`), it initiates an automatic seamless route failover.
   - Preserves non-prejudicial routing across all global geographic egresses based strictly on empirical capacity.

4. **Dual Native Implementations**:
   - **Android**: Native Kotlin + Go (Xray-core + Tun2Socks + WireGuard).
   - **Windows**: Modern desktop application built on Tauri v2 + Rust + Xray-core + Wintun driver (portable, standalone).

- **Latest Release (v2.3.44)**: \[REDACTED\]
- **Web & Live Node Feeds**: \[REDACTED\]

We welcome feedback, code contributions, and benchmark observations from researchers and circumvention developers operating in various filtered network topologies.

issues.title: Forged packet injection against QUIC SNI x.com, China, since 2026-11-17
issues.body:
## Prior QUIC block

Please see [Exposing and Circumventing SNI-based QUIC Censorship of the Great Firewall of China](https://gfw.report/publications/usenixsecurity25/en/) published July 2025. Summary:

1. The GFW decrypt SNI in QUIC `CRYPTO` payload with easily obtained key.
2. The GFW drops packets against 3-tuple for 180 seconds after seeing targeted SNI.
3. The block can be bypassed by splitting the SNI across multiple QUIC `CRYPTO`.
4. The blocklist differs with TLS SNI list.

## New packet injection behavior

Since the [direction connection to x.com tweet](https://x.com/k1uchanQ/status/2120471549828575281) got popular, the GFW technician soon patched the split SNI bypass bug and added new block strategy.

Block date source: https://x.com/rokedap50929384/status/2122477887492108319

```
curl --http3-only -v https://x.com \
--connect-to ::172.66.0.227 \
--curves X25519MLKEM768
```
```
*   Trying 172.66.0.227:443...
* SSL Trust Anchors:
*   CAfile: 
*   CApath: 
* QUIC connect to 172.66.0.227 port 443 failed: Weird server reply
* connect attempts inconclusive, retrying in 93ms
*   Trying 172.66.0.227:443...
* QUIC connect to 172.66.0.227 port 443 failed: Weird server reply
* connect attempts inconclusive, retrying in 114ms
*   Trying 172.66.0.227:443...
* QUIC connect to 172.66.0.227 port 443 failed: Weird server reply
* connect attempts inconclusive, retrying in 161ms
*   Trying 172.66.0.227:443...
* QUIC connect to 172.66.0.227 port 443 failed: Weird server reply
* connect attempts inconclusive, retrying in 101ms
*   Trying 172.66.0.227:443...
* QUIC connect to 172.66.0.227 port 443 failed: Weird server reply
* connect attempts inconclusive, retrying in 101ms
...
```

Based on packet capture I found the GFW would inject 2 fake QUIC packets, 1 `CONNECTION_CLOSE` frame followed by 1 `Version Negotiation`.

## Circumvention 

1. Ignore the forged UDP packets, they arrive abnormally soon, usually below 30ms, while real response from Cloudflare arrive in above 100ms.
2. Bogus CRYPTO or ACK frame injection from [CircumVolve: Automated Discovery of Censorship Evasion Strategies Using Large Language Models](https://gfw.report/publications/ccs26/en/#bogus-crypto-frame-frame-prefixing).
3. Send garbage packets before the first Initial, [`HINT_ZERO` in phantomsocks](https://github.com/macronut/phantomsocks/blob/0c47adb0495f697aa4030c93396ed71fed87b0e5/phantomtcp/quic.go#L1631). With this even SNI split is not needed.

## Pcap files

* 36 pairs of forged packets against x.com: [gfw-x.com-quic-injection.pcap.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35282736/gfw-x.com-quic-injection.pcap.zip)
* Control capture, `cloudflare.com` SNI to the same IP address: [gfw-x.com-quic-sni-control-benign-sni-same-ip.pcap.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35282734/gfw-x.com-quic-sni-control-benign-sni-same-ip.pcap.zip)
* Bypass the block with garbage packets: [gfw-x.com-quic-hint-zero-bypass.pcap.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/35282735/gfw-x.com-quic-hint-zero-bypass.pcap.zip)

issues.body:
When doing some testing today (2026-11-21), I noticed that `https://coconut.incognet.io/i2pseeds.su3` contains 100 zip entries, all of which were zero bytes in length (e.g. `routerInfo-j0eELJO7ndA9c4A95NE-T~F4mXI-3aM4c5gTd0xOy4o=.dat`). The other default reseed servers seemed to be fine.

This results in several "Identity: Buffer length 0 is too small" errors when a new router attempts to reseed from it (so, to be precise, about 100 log entries), which makes it look like a memory problem.

I guess some potential solutions here include removing this reseed server until the issue is fixed, or just skipping entries in `Reseeder::ProcessZIPStream` that decompress to fewer bytes than a minimal identity, with only one log warning shown per bundle to prevent log spam.

comments.issue_title: Add b64 check acceptable symbols
comments.body:
Thanks for working on this. As written the check only validates one character out of every four, so most invalid input still gets through.

The decode loop consumes 4 chars per iteration (the four `iT64[uint8_t(*ps++)]` reads), but `if (!IsBase64(*ps)) return 0;` runs once per iteration and inspects only the first char of each group (offsets 0, 4, 8, ...). An invalid char at any other offset is not checked. The test string `dG/z.A==` passes only because its invalid `.` happens to land at offset 4.

Built against this change, these are all still accepted (return 6 instead of 0):

```
A.AAAAAA   .  at offset 1
AA.AAAAA   .  at offset 2
AAA.AAAA   .  at offset 3
A/AAAAAA   /  (not in the i2p alphabet) at offset 1
```

To cover every position, validate each consumed character rather than just the group start. Note `IsBase64` cannot be applied per-char as-is: the loop also reads the `=` padding (via P64), and `IsBase64('=')` is false, so that would reject valid padded input such as `TQ==`. The reverse table already encodes validity - `iT64[...] == -1` marks an invalid symbol while padding maps to 0 - so testing the lookup result (or `IsBase64(c) || c == P64`) for each of the four reads handles both. Test vectors with the bad char at each of the four offsets would catch the regression.

issues.body:

- [X] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [X] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

**Cause**

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).

issues.title: VLESS Multiplex, Reverse Proxy: Refactor to move code into VLESS; Mux only uses `settings.multiplex` in VLESS/VMess outbound
issues.body:
This PR moves Multiplex to `proxy/vless/multiplex` and VLESS Reverse to `proxy/vless/reverse`. VLESS, VMess, and Reverse share the same Multiplex implementation. These paths pass decoded traffic through `DispatchLink` without intermediate `pipe` links.

### Protocol support

**Outbound Multiplex is available for VLESS and VMess.** Other outbound protocols use ordinary connections. VMess uses the shared implementation for inbound and outbound Mux. Ordinary VMess TCP and UDP keep the direct path from #5143. Reverse now uses the VLESS implementation, and the old standalone Reverse application has been removed.

### VLESS and VMess outbound configuration

Add `multiplex` under `outbounds[].settings`, alongside the protocol's other settings. This fragment enables the shared pool for up to eight active streams per connection.

```json
{
  "settings": {
    "multiplex": {
      "concurrency": 8,
      "xudpConcurrency": 0,
      "xudpProxyUDP443": "reject"
    }
  }
}
```

- A positive `concurrency` enables the shared pool. A positive `xudpConcurrency` enables a separate XUDP pool. If only `xudpConcurrency` is positive, TCP uses ordinary connections. With `xudpConcurrency` omitted or zero, UDP uses the shared pool when available.
- Omit `multiplex` or leave both counts at zero to use ordinary connections. An empty object `{}` also leaves Multiplex off. The old `enabled` property has no effect. Negative counts are rejected.
- `xudpProxyUDP443` applies when there is a pool for UDP/443. The default `reject` reports `XUDP rejected UDP/443 traffic`. `skip` uses the ordinary path, and `allow` uses the pool. UDP/443 uses the ordinary path when there is no applicable pool.
- XDrive requires a positive `concurrency` unless Reverse opens its own carrier. The shared XDrive pool uses a minimum concurrency of `128`.

### Legacy settings and API

Xray ignores the top-level `outbounds[].mux` key. During JSON loading it writes one warning to standard output per outbound containing that key, including when `settings.multiplex` is also present. The new settings determine whether Multiplex is enabled.

> The legacy "mux" setting is ignored. To enable Multiplex for VLESS or VMess outbounds, use "settings.multiplex". If Multiplex is disabled, Xray will use ordinary outbound connections.

API clients set `multiplex` in the VLESS or VMess outbound protocol configuration. The old `SenderConfig.multiplex_settings` field is ignored.

issues.title: XHTTP: bound TLS handshakes on TCP connections
issues.body:
The ChatGPT desktop app stopped loading workspace settings after an upgrade from one Wayrill version to the next. Restarting Wayrill routing, which restarted Xray, restored access. The traffic log showed the expected policy group, which includes XHTTP over TLS/HTTP/2 outbounds. The app reconnected normally as soon as the next upgrade, to Wayrill 0.37.17 with this patch, finished. The original capture begins after startup, so the evidence for the TLS stall comes from the controlled reproduction below.

## Reproduction and relation to #6590

The loopback reproduction uses an Xray VLESS/XHTTP client and server with the default three XMUX clients. A TCP relay accepts the first three connections, reads each TLS ClientHello and leaves those sockets open without sending a ServerHello. The relay forwards every new connection to the healthy Xray server. HTTP/2 requests sharing a pending dial keep waiting on the old sockets, even after the original application requests time out. Fresh requests then fail despite a working server being available to fresh dials.

This is the same stalled handshake reported in #6590. The additional finding is that the failure can persist across application retries after the peer is healthy for new connections. A TCP stack can keep acknowledging probes while the application or an intermediary makes no progress on a particular TLS handshake. The reproduction uses default TCP keepalive settings and injects a transient fault in the relay. [Closing discussion](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/6590#issuecomment-5178980812)

## Fix

Start a ten-second child context once the TCP connection is established, using the same handshake budget as Go's default HTTP transport. Complete standard TLS explicitly and use the same context for uTLS and REALITY. On expiry the stalled handshake ends and releases the socket, so HTTP/2 can retire the shared pending dial and subsequent requests can dial again. The context ends at handshake completion. Established streams continue under the existing HTTP request lifetime, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC's own handshake timeout.

## Validation

- On upstream `main` at `5d17b872`, six fresh requests timed out over 10.5 seconds. The relay saw no new dials. Restarting the client core restored traffic.
- With the patch, all three stalled sockets closed and a fresh request returned HTTP 200 in the same process. Verified this with Go TLS, uTLS and REALITY over HTTP/2. Also verified that the stalled sockets closed over HTTP/1.1.
- Verified healthy streams transferred data after 12 seconds in each of those configurations. The XHTTP Go suite passed alongside a local regression covering all three TLS paths against silent peers.

issues.title: SOCKS: prevent crash on failed UDP ASSOCIATE replies
issues.body:
A SOCKS5 client resetting its TCP control connection during UDP ASSOCIATE setup can crash the entire Xray process. `handshake5` creates the UDP association before writing the success reply. If that write fails, its error path calls `TempUDPConn.Close()`, but `processTCP` only installs the idle timer after the handshake returns successfully. `Close()` dereferences the nil timer instead of releasing the sockets and returning the connection error.

This is reachable with valid network input and default timeouts. In a controlled Windows/amd64 loopback reproduction against unmodified v26.10.17 (`92ccc939`), a client completed SOCKS authentication, sent UDP ASSOCIATE, and reset the TCP connection while setup was in progress. Xray exited with code 2 after one canceled request, with this stack:

```text
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
common/signal.(*ActivityTimer).SetTimeout
proxy/socks.(*TempUDPConn).Close
proxy/socks.(*ServerSession).handshake5
app/proxyman/inbound.(*tcpWorker).callback
```

Check whether the timer exists before stopping it. Let the timeout callback close the immutable socket pair directly, since the callback can run before `CancelAfterInactivity` returns and assigns `c.Timer` (synchronously for a zero timeout). Existing socket/configuration behavior is otherwise unchanged.

The regression test completes authentication and deterministically fails the UDP reply write, exercising the actual handshake error path. It panics before the fix and returns the original write error after it. Additional cases verify both sockets are closed before timer initialization, on immediate/normal idle expiry, and on explicit close with an active timer.

Validation on Windows/amd64, Go 1.27.2:

- `go test -mod=readonly ./proxy/socks ./proxy/http ./common/signal ./app/proxyman/inbound -count=1 -timeout=180s` passed.
- The UDP-association regressions passed 100 shuffled repetitions.
- A fresh core build with the fix handled 1,000 canceled UDP setups without exiting and then completed a UDP echo roundtrip through a new association. This controlled comparison establishes the trigger and the fix; it does not estimate production failure frequency.
- `go vet ./proxy/socks ./common/signal`, upstream `vformat`, and `git diff --check` passed.
- SOCKS tests cross-compiled for Linux/amd64 and macOS/arm64. Execution on those platforms, the race detector and the full suite remain unrun locally.

XMC: 20 Hz tick-driven data shaping / XMC：20Hz 按 tick 驱动的数据整形
issues.body:
> **Revision note / 修订说明**
>
> This issue originally proposed splitting the XMC config into `clients`/`servers` blocks. After the discussion (RPRX: the split has no clear advantage yet, keep the config as-is; switch the data path to 20 Hz instead, breaking is fine), the split was dropped and the PR #7456 was repurposed. To avoid opening a duplicate issue, this issue is updated in place: the title and description now track the 20 Hz data shaping.
>
> 本 issue 最初提出把 XMC 配置拆成 `clients`/`servers` 区块。讨论后（RPRX：暂时没看到拆分的明显优势，配置先别动；改为 20Hz 发数据，可以 breaking），拆分方案已放弃，#7456 也随之改成了 20Hz 实现。为避免再开一个重复 issue，这里直接原地更新标题和说明，改为跟踪 20Hz 数据整形。

### Problem / 问题

After the login/configuration handshake, XMC currently wraps proxy writes in `xmc:data` custom payloads immediately (up to 24 KiB each). An idle connection therefore emits no packets, and a busy one becomes a bulk TCP stream.

Real Minecraft is not a bandwidth-driven stream; it is a 20 TPS (50 ms) clock:

- both directions keep sending small packets even while idle (the client's per-tick packet, the server's entity/world updates);
- [Tick#Game process](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tick#Game_process) flushes queued packets once per tick;
- chunk loading is tick-shaped too: [Chunk Batch Received](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Received) reports a "chunks per tick" rate, the server waits for batch acknowledgements, and [Chunk Batch Finished](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Finished) targets roughly half of the available bandwidth;
- the 26.3 capture in #7423 shows packet rates near multiples of 20/s in both directions: idle c2s 21 pkt/s / 89 B/s, s2c 41 pkt/s / 5.6 KB/s; running 43/697 and 99/69K; join 2.2 MB / 12 s.

XMC 目前握手完成后会立即把代理写入封成 `xmc:data` 载荷（每块最多 24 KiB）：空闲时没有包，忙时就是一条 bulk TCP 流。

真实 Minecraft 不是带宽驱动的流，而是 20 TPS（50ms）的时钟：

- 空闲时双向也持续有小包（客户端每 tick 的包、服务端的实体/世界更新）；
- [Tick#Game process](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tick#Game_process) 每 tick 才 flush 一次队列里的包；
- 区块加载同样按 tick 整形：[Chunk Batch Received](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Received) 上报的是 "chunks per tick"，服务端要等 batch ack，[Chunk Batch Finished](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Java_Edition_protocol/Packets#Chunk_Batch_Finished) 还把目标压在约一半带宽；
- #7423 的 26.3 抓包显示双向包率都接近 20/s 的整数倍：挂机 c2s 21 包/s / 89 B/s、s2c 41 包/s / 5.6 KB/s；跑动 43/697 与 99/69K；进服 2.2 MB / 12 s。

### Proposal / 方案（implemented in #7456）

After the handshake, queue proxy writes and flush them once per 50 ms game tick:

- every tick writes one small `xmc:pad` frame, so an idle connection keeps the 20 Hz cadence in both directions;
- queued data is split into `xmc:data` payloads of at most 24 KiB and emitted inside the same tick batch;
- no artificial bandwidth cap: a busy tick may carry several payloads, like a Minecraft chunk burst;
- `Close` flushes the queued tick before closing the connection, so the last bytes are not dropped.

The startup `paddings` schedule and the configuration format are unchanged. This is a breaking wire change for XMC (old and new peers do not pair), which is acceptable for a finalmask mask.

握手完成后把代理写入入队，每 50ms 游戏 tick flush 一次：

- 每个 tick 固定发一个小 `xmc:pad` 帧，保证空闲时双向都有 20Hz 节拍；
- 队列数据按 24 KiB 拆成 `xmc:data` 载荷，在同一个 tick 批次里发出；
- 不设人为带宽上限：忙的 tick 可以带多个载荷，像 MC 的区块 burst；
- `Close` 前先 flush 队列，避免最后几个字节丢失。

启动阶段的 `paddings` 预置和配置格式不变。对 XMC 是 breaking 的线格式变更（新旧端不能互配），对 finalmask 来说可以接受。

### Scope / 范围

- One padding frame per tick per direction for now; the packet-count/size distribution is not yet state-dependent (idle/walk/loading).
- The vanilla chunk-batch/credit shape is not reproduced yet; this change only adds the 20 Hz cadence.
- The config split (`clients`/`servers`) is dropped; see the revision note.

- 还没复刻 vanilla 的 chunk batch/信用窗口，仅加入 20Hz 节拍；

issues.title: Downlink counter retains bytes from a failed write after a client disconnect
issues.body:
In a diagnostic run of standalone Xray-core, the per-user downlink counter retained 49,152 bytes after `WriteMultiBuffer` failed. The server accepted another 458,752 bytes in successful TLS writes, and the client had yet to read them when it stopped. issues.title: REALITY: per-SNI target, so SNI routing does not need an external L4 proxy (JARM goes to zeros)
issues.body:
Related: #2374, #5420, #2108.

#2374 asked for this and was answered with "use an L4 proxy". The catch: with nginx/haproxy ssl_preread in front, JARM of the server returns all zeros, which is exactly the server-side fingerprint REALITY exists to avoid. So SNI routing currently costs the property it is supposed to protect.

Proposal: allow a target per serverName, resolved inside REALITY.

"realitySettings": {
  "target": "default.example:443",
  "targets": { "other.example": "other.example:443" },
  "serverNames": ["default.example", "other.example"]
}

Pick the splice target from the received SNI; fall back to `target` when there is no match; keep configs without `targets` unchanged. Also fixes the cert mismatch: today every extra serverName gets the default target's certificate, which is invalid for that name and breaks plain-TLS clients and probes on it (see YouzSpace/3xui-hub#38).

Watch: read the SNI before splicing without an extra round trip; only allow targets present in serverNames; keep record sizes and timings identical.

Also worth documenting: fallbacks are not evaluated on REALITY inbounds (#5420), so `path`-based fallback is not an alternative.

issues.title: Hysteria, MASQUE, XDRIVE & XHTTP/3 clients: Close the packet conn before the QUIC transport
issues.body:
When a client dials through `sockopt.dialerProxy`, its packet conn is a `FakePacketConn` over `cnc.Connection`, and `SetReadDeadline` on it does nothing. `quic.Transport.Close()` stops its read loop only through that deadline and then waits for the loop to return, so closing the transport before the packet conn blocks until the tunnel under it closes by itself.

In the Hysteria client this happens in `client.close()` with the client lock held, so every new dial on that outbound waits. I hit it with a Hysteria outbound behind another Hysteria outbound and an apernet Hysteria 2.14.0 server at the end (default `maxIdleTimeout` of 30s). After 35 seconds of idle the next request timed out, and the outbound stayed dead for about two minutes. With a request every 60 seconds it never recovered.

Fix: close the packet conn first, then the transport, as #7413 did for one XHTTP/3 path. This covers the Hysteria client and the same calls in MASQUE, XDRIVE and the XHTTP/3 `context.AfterFunc`. With the fix, the Hysteria setup above reconnects on the first request after idle: 0 failures in 36 requests, against two-minute stalls before.

issues.title: XTLS Vision: Track TLS record boundaries across writes
issues.body:
Fixes https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/issues/7164

`IsCompleteRecord` checks each write on its own, so once a write ends inside a record, no later write can pass. With back-to-back records Vision then pads the whole transfer. This is a smaller take on the idea in #7307: one function replaces `IsCompleteRecord`, and the diff is +53 −51 in `proxy/proxy.go` plus a test file.

`VisionWriter` keeps two fields: how many bytes of the current record are still to come, and the record's type. `tlsRecordEnd` walks the record headers in each write from that point. It returns the end of the last complete application data record (0 if the write holds a handshake record). The padding ends exactly there with `CommandPaddingDirect`, as #5179 requires. The rest of the write is written right after the switch, through the existing direct-copy path. If the stream is not TLS records, or a write ends inside a record header, tracking is lost. Each write is then checked from its first byte, as before.

The receiver and the wire format are unchanged, so old and new versions work together in both directions.

**Repro from #7164** (tlsblast, 1 GB, back-to-back 16 KiB records, VLESS + TLS + Vision over 127.0.0.1, `loglevel: warning`, macOS arm64, 3 runs; CPU is client + server seconds):

| 1 GB | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| upload | 3.1 Gbit/s, 2.0 + 3.6 s CPU | 12–15 Gbit/s, 0.5 + 0.6 s CPU |
| download | 2.4–3.4 Gbit/s, 3.4 + 1.8 s CPU | 11–16 Gbit/s, 0.6 + 0.6 s CPU |

At `loglevel: debug`, with 64 MiB per transfer:
- main: 16,408 `XtlsPadding` lines on the sender.
- This PR, upload: the client switches on its first write, ending the padding right after ChangeCipherSpec + Finished (`XtlsPadding 64 … 2`).
- This PR, download: the server ends the padding at the end of the first full application data record (`XtlsPadding 22 … 2`, 16,406 bytes in). It does not switch in the write that holds the handshake flight.
- All four main/PR client/server pairs complete. The speedup follows the patched sender's direction.

**Tests**
- New `proxy/vision_test.go`. It covers upload and download streams, cut by various batch sizes, and checks:
  - the padding ends with `CommandPaddingDirect` at the expected record boundary;
  - the padded part plus the raw part equals the original stream.

  It also has table cases for `tlsRecordEnd`. The writer test fails on main.
- `go test -race ./proxy/ ./proxy/vless/... ./proxy/freedom/... ./common/buf/...` passes.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios -run TestVless` passes, including `TestVlessXtlsVision` and `TestVlessXtlsVisionReality`.

---

中文简述：`IsCompleteRecord` 按单次写入判断，记录一旦跨写入就再也无法通过，背靠背的大记录会导致整个连接一直 padding。本 PR 在 `VisionWriter` 里记录当前 TLS 记录剩余的字节数和记录类型，在每次写入中找到最后一个完整 application data 记录的结尾：padding 恰好在记录边界结束（保持 #5179 的保证），剩余部分在切换后直接写出。不含握手记录的写入才会切换。接收端与协议格式不变，新旧版本互通。比 #7307 简单很多，只替换了一个函数。

issues.title: XDRIVE: delete S3 objects before their parent directories
issues.body:
Fixes #7428.

XDRIVE's S3 cleanup deletes the session key before listing its children. On a backend that rejects deletion of nonempty directories, the first DELETE returns HTTP 412 and cleanup stops. This change collects the keys under the session prefix across all list pages and deletes them in reverse lexicographic order. Each child is deleted before its directory marker, and the session key is deleted last. Cleanup holds one key string per listed object in memory.

## Reproduction

`TestS3DeleteNonemptyDirectory` uses the production S3 client against a local HTTP test server. The server returns 412 for a DELETE while the directory has children. It lists the `abc/up/` marker on the first page and its segment on the second. After deleting session `abc`, the test checks that the only remaining key belongs to the neighboring session `abcd`.

git archive 82b5b76b | tar -x -C "$before"
cp transport/internet/xdrive/s3_test.go "$before/transport/internet/xdrive/"
(cd "$before" && go test -count=1 -run '^TestS3DeleteNonemptyDirectory$' ./transport/internet/xdrive)

issues.title: XDRIVE: Prevent ring-slot reuse before the previous upload completes
issues.body:
## Problem

The peer can acknowledge segment 0 from the inline session announcement while its upload to the ring is still in flight. With a ring of depth 2, that acknowledgement can admit the upload for segment 2 to the same slot. If the original upload finishes last, it overwrites segment 2 and leaves a gap in the stream.

This ordering reproduces the intermittent `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` failure seen in two Ubuntu jobs. [November 13 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43400976127/job/131803491599) and [November 14 job](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/actions/runs/43647865009/job/132609573715).

## Fix

- Require a successful previous write to the same slot and an acknowledgement from the existing cumulative watermark before reusing it.
- Keep checking the watermark while the local upload is pending. The reader-stall timeout applies while the acknowledgement is missing, so an acknowledged upload can finish retrying during `Close`.
- Propagate a terminal write error to queued reuse of the slot and retain the best-effort error frame for peers still waiting for that sequence.

The change uses the existing announcement, frame format, and acknowledgement protocol.

## Validation

- Extended `TestSlotFirstAnnouncement` to hold the first upload after the inline acknowledgement. The slow-write case verifies the complete byte stream through EOF. The failure case verifies that `Close` promptly returns the original write error and that the slot contains the error frame.
- Verified that the regression test detects premature reuse on upstream `main`. Both cases passed 100 times with the race detector on this branch.
- Passed the full `transport/internet/xdrive` suite on Windows with and without `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

Happy Eyeballs: add successDefinition to race until TLS handshake completes
issues.body:
## Motivation

When the server's domain resolves to several IPs, Happy Eyeballs is supposed to pick a working one. In Russia, however, some ISPs (the DPI boxes installed at them) drop the ServerHello for some of these IPs while TCP to them still connects. Which IPs are affected differs from one ISP and region to another and changes over time: an IP that is blocked for one client works for another, so removing it from DNS would only break it for everyone else. Happy Eyeballs today ends the race at the first TCP connection, so it happily picks such an IP, and then the TLS or REALITY handshake can never complete. A retry usually picks the same IP again, because it wins the TCP race again. In this situation the current Happy Eyeballs is of no use at all, even though other IPs of the same domain work fine.

## What this PR adds

A new optional field `successDefinition` in `sockopt.happyEyeballs`:

| Value | The race is won by |
|---|---|
| `tcpConnected` (default) | the first established TCP connection, as before |
| `tlsHandshakeComplete` | the first connection that completes the TLS or REALITY handshake |

```json
"sockopt": {
  "domainStrategy": "UseIP",
  "happyEyeballs": {
    "tryDelayMs": 250,
    "maxConcurrentTry": 4,
    "successDefinition": "tlsHandshakeComplete"
  }
}
```

Without `successDefinition`, or with `tcpConnected`, nothing changes. Without TLS or REALITY, `tlsHandshakeComplete` is the same as `tcpConnected`.

The behaviour follows section 6.1 of Happy Eyeballs v3, which says clients SHOULD wait for the TLS handshake to complete before canceling other attempts: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-happy-happyeyeballs-v3/
Chromium's Happy Eyeballs v3 implementation does the same: a TCP-based attempt runs the TLS handshake inside it and completes only when the handshake does, and an attempt counts as slow (so the next one starts) if TCP and TLS together take longer than the connection attempt delay:
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/socket/tls_stream_attempt.cc
- https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/net/http/http_stream_pool_attempt.cc

Happy Eyeballs v3 is still a draft, and browsers do not use it by default yet: in Chromium it is behind the `HappyEyeballsV3` feature, which is disabled by default, and Firefox enables it only in Nightly.

## How it works

- The scheduler of `TcpRaceDial` is reused as is (`tryDelayMs`, `maxConcurrentTry`, `prioritizeIPv6`, `interleave`); only the attempt it runs differs. With `tcpConnected` the attempt is the same system dial as before.
- With `tlsHandshakeComplete` every attempt goes through TCP dial to one IP → FinalMask (if any) → the transport's own TLS or REALITY handshake. Only the TCP destination changes from attempt to attempt; masks apply to each attempt separately, exactly as on a normal dial.
- An attempt keeps its `maxConcurrentTry` slot until its handshake ends, and a hanging handshake does not stop the scheduler from starting the next attempt after `tryDelayMs`.
- Losing attempts are stopped by closing their connections. Transports that leave the handshake to the first write (gRPC, and HTTPUpgrade and XHTTP with Go TLS) get it completed inside the race, so a connection is never handshaked twice.
- The race happens under the same conditions as the TCP race in `DialSystem`: `domainStrategy` set, at least two IPs, no `dialerProxy`, non-zero `tryDelayMs` and `maxConcurrentTry`. Otherwise the transport dials exactly as before.

All covered transports now dial through `internet.DialTCPWithHandshake(ctx, dest, streamSettings, handshake)`. `handshake` is a function that wraps the TCP connection with the transport's TLS or REALITY client; it holds the same code the transport used to run right after its own TCP dial.

Transports covered: RAW (TLS, REALITY), WebSocket, HTTPUpgrade, gRPC (TLS, REALITY), XHTTP over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS, REALITY), MASQUE over HTTP/2. For XHTTP the race runs once per new physical connection. UDP

TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
issues.body:
## Why

With Xray's TUN as the system VPN, an app that reads a response until the server closes waits about 1 s more than it should on every such connection. The outbound already knows the response is over, but TUN keeps the app's connection open until the whole dispatch ends, and that happens only after `uplinkOnly`. Examples are HTTP/1.0 without `Content-Length`, RTSP (Moonlight in #5845) and simple request and reply protocols. With this change the app gets the end of the response right away

## What changed

- TUN sends FIN to the app as soon as the outbound is done with the response. The app can still send, and the connection is closed as before when the dispatch is over
- the lightweight TCP stack gets `CloseWrite` for that
- the rest of the core still closes links in pairs, as agreed in the thread

## Testing and limits

- `TestTCPCloseWrite` checks that FIN goes out, that data from the app is still read after it and that `Close` sends nothing more. `go test -race ./proxy/tun` passes
- this helps only when the outbound itself sees the end of the response, for example freedom or VMess. Over VLESS the outbound ends only after `uplinkOnly` on the server, so the wait there stays

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

issues.title: XHTTP server: unblock writes and serialize connection close
issues.body:
## Summary

An XHTTP response write can hold the connection mutex while blocked on a slow reader. Closing the logical connection then waits on that mutex, including when a proxy inactivity timeout cancels the business context while the HTTP request stays open.

Signal closure before waiting for the writer and interrupt an active write using `http.ResponseController`. Serialize the complete transition with `sync.Once` so concurrent business/handler closes join the deadline call and the writer before `ServeHTTP` returns.

```text
Close (once)
  signal closure
  interrupt active write
  wait for writer completion
```

## Evidence

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: Finalmask: Add the `lua` mask (noise's `script` moves there)
issues.body:
#7174 bolted a second Lua mask onto header-custom, which was the wrong way around. One `lua` mask covers all of it now: it is both a `tcpMasks` and a `udpMasks` entry, and the script decides what it does by the hooks it defines.

-- `HandleHeader(stream, address, role)`, TCP: a free handshake before any traffic, with `stream:Write`, `stream:Read` and `stream:Sleep`. Return a string or an error and the connection is dropped
-- `HandleHeaderWrite(header, address, role)` and `HandleHeaderRead(packet, address, role)`, UDP: prefix every packet with a header, and strip it on the other side by returning its length, or `nil` to drop the packet
-- `HandleNoise(plan, address, role)` is the old noise hook, so `noise`'s `script` is gone (it has not been in a release yet)
-- `role` is `client` or `server`, so one file serves both ends
-- a hook the script does not define is not wrapped at all: a noise only script leaves TCP connections alone and never touches a packet
-- the module is `xray.finalmask` now, with `Random` and `RandomBetween`

```json
{
    "udpMasks": [{"type": "lua", "settings": {"script": "mask.lua", "reset": "30-60"}}]
}
```

Per call it takes at most 64 noise packets and 65535 bytes of noise, 1024 bytes of header, and 65535 bytes each way in a handshake. A packet hook gets 1s, a handshake 30s. A UDP header is one Lua call per packet, the benchmarks in the package cover its cost.

The static lists can follow later, the same script can already do what they do.

XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Outbound: Close the handler when removing it; VLESS Reverse Proxy: Don't start after closing
issues.body:
`outbound.Manager.RemoveHandler`, which `xray api rmo` (`HandlerService.RemoveOutbound`) calls, deletes the handler from the map but never closes it, while `inbound.Manager.RemoveHandler` does. So whatever the removed outbound's `Close()` would release keeps running:

- WireGuard creates its TUN in the constructor (a kernel TUN when available, otherwise a gVisor stack), and once used also has the device with its UDP socket and keepalives.
- VLESS with `reverse` keeps its monitor task: the removed outbound keeps dialing the server every 2 s.
- Same for MASQUE's tunnel. VLESS with `testpre` gets closed too, but its pre-connects only stop reliably with #7113: on main, `Close()` stops just the goroutines waiting to hand over a connection, not the ones redialing an unreachable server.

This shows up wherever outbounds are added and removed at runtime through the API, e.g. by panels.

### Changes

- `RemoveHandler` closes the handler it removed. It does so after releasing the manager lock, so a slow `Close()` (WireGuard) doesn't hold up `Select()`/`GetHandler()` for new connections. Removing an unknown tag still returns nil, and a removed handler is closed only once, since `Manager.Close()` no longer sees it.
- VLESS starts the reverse 2 s after the outbound is created (a goroutine in `New()`), so an outbound removed within those 2 s would still start it after `Close()`. `Reverse.Start()` is now a no-op once `Reverse.Close()` has run.

The other callers of `RemoveHandler` (commander, metrics, reverse portal, VLESS inbound's reverse) remove their own internal outbounds, whose `Close()` is a no-op or idempotent.

Connections already in flight on a removed outbound behave as before unless its `Close()` tears them down (WireGuard, MASQUE). A reverse bridge that is already connected is left to end on its own; only new ones stop.

### Reproduction (on 836a6fe)

Client: `api` with `HandlerService` behind a dokodemo-door inbound, `freedom` as the only configured outbound. Server: a plain TCP listener that only counts accepted connections.

**VLESS `reverse`**: the outbound is added with `xray api ado` and removed with `xray api rmo`. Afterwards `xray api lso` lists only the `freedom` outbound in all runs.

| `rmo` after `ado` | build | accepts at `rmo` | 3 s later | 13 s later |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 s | main | 3 | 4 | 9 |
| 7 s | this PR | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| 0.5 s | main | 0 | 1 | 6 |
| 0.5 s | this PR | 0 | 0 | 0 |

**WireGuard** (`noKernelTun: true`): five outbounds, each added with `ado` and removed right away with `rmo`. Goroutines from the `metrics` listener's `/debug/pprof/goroutine`: main 11 → 72, this PR 11 → 12.

### Tests

- New `TestRemoveHandlerClosesHandler` (on main the handler is closed 0 times) and `TestReverseNotStartedAfterClose` (on main the monitor runs once).
- `go test ./...` except `testing/scenarios`: the only failures also fail on main, tests that need `resources/geo*.dat` or network access.
- `go test ./testing/scenarios`: pass.
- `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check -pwd ./`: pass.

issues.title: Bound shutdown after termination signal
issues.body:
This change prevents Xray from waiting indefinitely during graceful shutdown after receiving SIGTERM or interrupt.

Previously, shutdown depended on the deferred server.Close() call returning. If any feature Close() path blocked, the process could stay alive while listeners or active connections continued operating. This made stale Xray processes difficult to detect, especially when another process could bind the same port.

Now Xray runs server.Close() explicitly after receiving a termination signal and waits up to 10 seconds. If shutdown does not complete in time, the process exits with code 1 so supervisors can treat it as a failed shutdown and avoid leaving a functional stale process behind.

This issue was most visible on mobile clients. Some apps, such as Telegram proxy-style traffic, may continue using an already-established path even when the VPN/client UI appears disabled. If the old Xray process remains alive during a stuck shutdown, those connections can continue transferring traffic and updating usage counters, making the node look stopped from the client side while traffic is still flowing server-side.

issues.title: TLS : tls spoofing
issues.body:
fix #5964

### RawPacket aka TLS Spoofing

So first lets talk about the idea,

when you connect to a xray server, the censors can see your TLS ClientHello, read the SNI, and figure out what you are doing and block :)

The RawPacket aka TLS spoofing fixes that by injecting a fake TLS ClientHello before the real one Hits.


The fake one carries like a decoy domain (ex. baidu.com) and then the real one carries your actual destination (ex. www.example.com).

A sensor that captures the first packet sees baidu.com and think that you are just browsing, and everything is okay with that, but in reality your connection goes through :)


It can be configured in the `finalmask.tcp` okay? and its only for client side.


### How everything works


When Xray dials a TCP connection and the first `Write()` happens (which also triggers the real TLS handshake) , our Raw Packet setup does the following.

1.builds a fake Tls ClientHello with whatever SNI you want or you have option to provide the raw bytes (b64).

2.Then we. wrap it in a raw TCP/ip packet.

3.Then deliberately we corrupt the TCP header using whatever method is selected okay?

4. Then we shoot it out via a raw socket

5. Then immediately let the real `Write()` go through normally


In short : two packets arrive at the server back to back and the fake one gets dropped by the servers TCP stack because of the corruption and then the real handshake proceeds like nothing happened.


### Config Example

```json
{
  "streamSettings": {
    "finalmask": {
      "tcp": [
        {
          "type": "rawpacket",
          "settings": {
            "sni": "baidu.com",
            "payload": "",
            "method": "wrong-sequence",
            "ttl": 3,
            "count": 1
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```


### Available Fields

`sni` : The domain to put in the fake ClientHello. If you set this, it will auto generate a valid TLS ClientHello for you automatically. If you set `payload` and `sni` same time , sni wins here.

```
"sni": "baidu.com"
```

`payload` : If you don't want an auto gnrated ClientHello, then just encode your raw bytes that you want into base64 and put them here. I have added an option to do it from command line also. Do like this 

```
 xray tls fake-hello google.com
 ```

It will out the thing and then just copy paste.


Note : If `sni` and payload are empty or not set , the raw packet does nothing and the connection goes through normally.


`method` : It defines how we corrupt the fake packet so the server drops it.

`wrong-sequence` : It duplicates the sequence number (looks like a retransmission so server drops it)

So we grab the kernels `snd_nxt` ( the next sequence number the kernel expects to send), then subtract the length of the fake payload and then use that as the sequence number of the injected packet. The results then is a duplicate of the. last segment, so the receivers TCP stack sees it as a retransmit at best, or like out of window at worst and then drops it.


`wrong-checksum`: It flips all the bits in the TCP checksum (so server sees a bad checksum and drops it)

We build the packet with a correct checksum and then flip every bit(^0xFFFF). The receiver then validates the checksum and its wrong, so the packet goes in trash.

`wrong-ack`: It sets ACK number way outside the receive window (so server sends dup ACK then drops it)

It sets the ACK number to `rcv_nxt - window/2` and that's way outside of the receivers window, and the kernel responds with a dup ACK containing the correct sequence number, then drops it.

`wrong-md5` : This adds a fake TCP MD5 signature option and server without MD5 drops it

Here we append a TCP option with kind=19 and length=18 to the TCP header. The kind 19 is the MD5 signature option (RFC 2385), if the receiver doesn't use TCP MD5 (which is basically everything except some BGP routers), it sees an unknown option

Refs #7455. The config split proposed there was dropped after the discussion; this PR now only contains the 20 Hz data shaping.

## What changed

After the login/configuration handshake, proxy writes are queued and flushed once per 50 ms game tick instead of being wrapped in custom payloads immediately:

- every tick writes one small padding frame on `xmc:pad`, so an idle connection keeps the same 20 Hz cadence as a real client in both directions;
- queued proxy data is split into `xmc:data` payloads of at most 24 KiB and emitted inside the same tick batch, so a busy connection looks like per-tick bursts instead of a bulk TCP stream;
- `Close` flushes the queued tick before closing, so the last bytes of a graceful shutdown are not dropped;

issues.title: XDRIVE: Cancel pending storage operations on interrupt
issues.body:
## Problem

`common.Interrupt` falls back to `Close()` for an XDRIVE connection. `Close()` drains the writer before canceling the connection context. If storage is holding an upload, interruption waits for the very operation it needs to cancel. The asynchronous slot announcement also uses a background context, so it can remain pending after connection shutdown.

svlavr reported both behaviors while testing direct VLESS multiplexing. A mock backend reproduced them with a held upload and a held announcement. [Original report in #7415](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7415#issuecomment-6886431076)

## Design

`Interrupt()` cancels the session before entering the existing `Close()` path. Cancellation runs before the `sync.Once` guard, so it can wake a graceful close that is already waiting. Both slot and WAL writers stop admitting work after cancellation and wait for in-flight writes to finish unwinding before storage is released. A canceled drain skips the EOF marker.

The slot announcement now uses the session context and is part of the writer’s existing wait group. The context makes an interrupted publication cancelable. Joining it also lets a short graceful transfer finish publishing its session before `Close()` sends EOF and releases storage. This keeps the inline first-segment optimization and the existing wire format.

`Close()` still means graceful drain. Transport owners use `common.Interrupt` on the underlying connection when they need to abort. The direct Mux proposal already unwraps stats connections on its explicit interrupt path. [#7364](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7364)

## Validation

- Added regressions for interrupting an already-running `Close()` with a blocked slot or WAL upload, canceling a pending announcement, and allowing the announcement to finish during graceful close. All four cases detect the original behavior on upstream `main`.
- Passed the full XDRIVE suite on Windows with and without `-race`, plus 50 race-enabled repetitions of the shutdown regressions.
- Trial-merged this branch with #7415 and ran both sets of regressions together 10 times under `-race`. Live cloud tests were skipped.

ye, it's stupid: Iranian firewall cuts XDNS as soon as the query names look like base32. One UDP socket to 1.1.1.1 gets about 16 answers and then nothing, while the same queries with other characters all go through.

This adds `alphabet` to `domains`: 32 unique chars from a-z0-9, set the same on both sides. Empty keeps the old base32, so existing configs don't change.

```jsonc
"domains": [{"names": ["t.example.com"], "alphabet": "v9u8t0s1rqponmlkjihgfedcba765432"}]
```

Tested on a TCI home line with one `udp://1.1.1.1:53` entry, two runs each:

- default: the handshake never finishes, 0 bytes

issues.title: Feature Request: Support a configurable Wintun adapter GUID on Windows
issues.body:
Currently, Xray-core derives the Wintun adapter GUID from the configured interface name using MD5:

id := md5.Sum([]byte(name))
guid := (*windows.GUID)(unsafe.Pointer(&id[0]))

This provides deterministic adapter identity based on the interface name, which works well for standard use cases.

However, there are scenarios where applications need to control the Wintun adapter identity independently of its display name.

I propose adding an optional "guid" field to the TUN inbound configuration, allowing users to specify a fixed Wintun adapter GUID on Windows.

Proposed Configuration

{
  "protocol": "tun",
  "settings": {
    "name": "xray0",
    "guid": "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "mtu": 1500
  }
}

The "guid" field would be optional.

- If specified, Xray-core uses the provided GUID when opening or creating the Wintun adapter.
- If omitted, Xray-core retains the existing behavior of deriving the GUID from the interface name using MD5.
- On non-Windows platforms, the field is ignored.

Motivation

A configurable GUID would be useful for applications managing multiple network engines, configurations, or profiles that need to coordinate access to a consistent Wintun adapter identity.

For example:

- Multiple engine instances sharing a common TUN device identity.
- Applications that need to identify an adapter independently of its display name.
- Maintaining adapter identity across interface renames or configuration changes.
- Integrations where the host application manages adapter lifecycle and needs predictable adapter identification.

Windows adapter identity and interface naming are separate concerns. Allowing an explicit GUID would provide additional flexibility without changing the default behavior.

Proposed Implementation

1. Add an optional "guid" string field to the TUN configuration in "infra/conf/tun.go".
2. Add the corresponding field to "proxy/tun/config.proto".
3. Regenerate the protobuf bindings.
4. Pass the GUID through "TunOptions".
5. Update the Windows implementation to use the provided GUID when present.
6. Preserve the existing MD5-based GUID generation as the fallback.
7. Accept and ignore the field on non-Windows platforms.

Backward Compatibility

This change would be fully backward-compatible.

Existing configurations would continue using the current MD5-based GUID derivation, with no changes to existing behavior.

Platform Support

This option would only have an effect on Windows, where Wintun adapter creation and identification use GUIDs.

Other platforms would ignore the option.

Additional Considerations

The supplied GUID should be validated as a canonical UUID.

Users should ensure that explicitly configured GUIDs do not conflict with GUIDs assigned to unrelated Wintun adapters.

The default behavior should remain unchanged to avoid breaking existing configurations.

Question

Would maintainers consider adding an optional, Windows-specific "guid" configuration field to the TUN inbound?

I would be happy to contribute an implementation if this feature is considered appropriate.

comments.issue_title: VLESS Multiplex, Reverse Proxy: Refactor to move code into VLESS; Mux only uses `settings.multiplex` in VLESS/VMess outbound
comments.body:
@RPRX Yes, I kept the XDrive minimum of **128 active Multiplex streams per physical connection** from #7375. With the shared pool enabled, XDrive still raises any lower value to 128.

<details>
<summary>Configuration details</summary>

- **Ordinary XDrive.** Set a positive `settings.multiplex.concurrency`. Values such as `8` and `64` are raised to `128`. Values of `128` or more are kept as configured.
- **Unset or zero.** An empty setting or `concurrency: 0` leaves the shared pool disabled, so ordinary XDrive rejects the configuration. With the old `mux` enabled, zero used to become `8` first, then `128` for XDrive.
- **Separate XUDP pool.** It uses its own `xudpConcurrency` value. For example, `8` stays `8`. An XUDP-only pool is insufficient for ordinary XDrive, which requires the shared pool.
- **XDrive with Reverse.** Reverse opens its own Multiplex carrier, so an explicit positive `concurrency` is optional.
- **Other transports.** The minimum of 128 is specific to XDrive. An explicit `8` or `64` remains the configured limit.
- **Legacy `mux`.** Xray warns and ignores the old key and its contents, including any negative values. If both keys are present, `settings.multiplex` determines the pool settings.
- **Negative values in `settings.multiplex`.** A negative `concurrency` or `xudpConcurrency` produces the error `multiplex "concurrency" and "xudpConcurrency" must be non-negative`. Xray fails to start with that JSON. An API `AddOutbound` request returns an error without adding the outbound.

</details>

| 方向 | id | 包 | 关键字段 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| c2s | 0x00 | hello | name, UUID |
| c2s | 0x01 | key | shared secret, verify token |
| c2s | 0x03 | login_acknowledged | 空 |
| s2c | 0x00 | disconnect | reason |
| s2c | 0x01 | hello | serverId, RSA 公钥, verify token, shouldAuthenticate |
| s2c | 0x02 | login_finished | GameProfile（26.2 起尾部多 16 字节 sessionId UUID） |
| s2c | 0x03 | compression | threshold varint |

加密是 AES/CFB8 + RSA-1024 PKCS#1 v1.5，767→777 没动过。

**4. 配置状态**

| 方向 | 用的 id | 包 | 备注 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| s2c | 0x01 | custom_payload | 数据流和 tick padding |
| c2s | 0x02 | custom_payload | 数据流 |
| 双向 | 0x04 | keep_alive | 长连接保活 |

其余包（registry_data、select_known_packs、cookie_request、26.x 的 dialog / code_of_conduct）我们**不按 id 处理**，读循环里遇到不认识的 id 直接读掉丢弃，所以它们的 id 变了也不影响——XMC 真正依赖的 id 只有这 4 个，这是它能跨版本撑住的原因。

custom payload 的大小上限是分方向的：clientbound 1 MiB（`ClientboundCustomPayloadPacket.MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE = 1048576`），serverbound 32767（`ServerboundCustomPayloadPacket.MAX_PAYLOAD_SIZE = 32767`）。所以数据流切 24 KiB、padding 帧切 32767，不是拍脑袋。

## 767 → 777 到底变了什么

包 id 不是抓来的，是 `ConfigurationProtocols` / `LoginProtocols` 里 `addPacket(...)` 的注册顺序，从各版本官方映射 jar 直接读。8 个版本的实测：

| MC | 协议 | 用到的 id | 配置包数 s2c/c2s | 登录包数 s2c/c2s | login_finished |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.21.1 | 767 | 全同 | 17 / 8 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 1.21.4 | 769 | 全同 | 17 / 8 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 1.21.5 | 770 | 全同 | 17 / 8 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 1.21.8 | 772 | 全同 | 19 / 9 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 1.21.11 | 774 | 全同 | 20 / 10 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 26.1 | 775 | 全同 | 20 / 10 | 6 / 5 | GameProfile |
| 26.2 | 776 | 全同 | 20 / 10 | 6 / 5 | **+UUID sessionId** |
| 26.3 | 777 | 全同 | **21** / 10 | 6 / 5 | +UUID sessionId |

三条结论：

1. **我们在用的每一个 id 都没变。** 现在能跑不是因为我们做对了什么，是因为插包恰好都落在 `0x04` 之后。
2. **列表在长**：配置状态 clientbound 从 17 涨到 21、serverbound 从 8 涨到 10，1.21.1 到 26.3 一共多了 6 个包。按这个速率，迟早有一次插到 `0x01`–`0x04` 前面。
3. **26.3 已经真的插在中间了**：`POST_EFFECTS` 落在 `0x0a`，把 `STORE_COOKIE` 往后顶了一位。要不是它在 keep-alive 之后，这次就破了。

## 不建表的话，追新版本有多难

现在的 id 是散在 4 个文件里的字面量：`client.go` 的 `protocolVersion = 775` 加 0x00/0x01/0x02/0x03，`server.go` 的 status JSON（写死 `"26.1.2"` / 775）和 0x00/0x01，`packet_stream.go` 的 0x01/0x02/0x04，`padding.go` 通过 `paddingFramePacketID` 再推导一次。加一个版本要动的是这些全部，而且：

- **没有变更日志可查。** 麻将的 release notes 不会告诉你"配置状态 clientbound 插入了一个包，id 后移"。唯一可靠的办法是拿新 jar 反编译、diff 注册顺序——这正是这次做的事。也就是说，每次版本更新都要重做一遍这次的分析，做的人还得知道 `ConfigurationProtocols` 在哪。
- **失败是运行时的，而且长得像网络问题。** id 错了不会编译报错，表现是登录阶段服务端把我们的包当成别的包处理、回一个奇怪的断开，或者客户端在配置阶段一直等。线上出现时没有任何信号指向"包 id 变了"。
- **一个二进制只能说一个协议号。** 现在写死 775，等于每支持一个新版本就得重新发一版 Xray，旧版本同时被丢掉。想同时服务多版本（模组有 9 个分支，现实里也不可能只留一个）就必须让协议号运行时可变，那本来就等于建表。
- **没法测试。** 字面量散在逻辑里，只能靠"连一次真服务器"验证；有表的话，表本身可以被单测钉住，再拿模组的不同分支跑一遍就闭环了。

粗略对比：有表的话追一个版本 ≈ 跑一次提取脚本加一行 + 跑一遍 e2e（半小时级）；没有表就是每次重新反编译、手改 5 处、再手工验证（小时级，且没有任何回归保护）。

## 打算怎么做

1. `protocolDesc` 表：每行协议号、版本名、登录/配置用到的 id、字段形状标记（`loginFinishedSessionId` 这种）。1.21+ 现在只有协议号不同，表看起来"没用"，但上面 0x0a 那个例子说它会用上。
2. 表从 jar 的注册顺序**生成**，不手抄：提取脚本留在仓库外也行，PR 里贴生成结果，评审时能对上来源。
3. 握手协议号从表取；服务端按收到的协议号选行；status 响应按配置/协商报版本。
4. 版本协商：默认 status ping 探测（nextState=1 读 `version.protocol` 再连），配置留手动覆盖。
5. 联调用模组那 9 个分支当服务器。

## 风险

- 配置阶段的"未答复任务"：`select_known_packs`、`cookie_request`、26.x 的 `code_of_conduct` 我们一律不答。Fabric/vanilla 容忍（现状已验），Paper/Velocity 类实现可能会等 ack 或超时。
- `login_finished` 26.2 加字段说明登录阶段还会继续加，客户端"读固定字段 + 忽略剩余"的容忍要一直保持。

comments.issue_title: XMC: 20 Hz tick-driven data shaping / XMC：20Hz 按 tick 驱动的数据整形
comments.body:
先把“MC 在底层长什么样”讲清楚，再回答拆分的问题。

**TL;DR**：MC 是 tick 驱动的（20 TPS / 50ms），空闲时也持续有包；TLS 是应用写入驱动的，可以长时间零包再突然满速。两者在 TCP 层的形状不是一回事。

### 1. MC 的节拍

- 游戏逻辑 20 TPS，也就是 50ms 一个 tick。
- 绝大多数包按 tick 产生：移动、实体同步、时间，以及客户端每 tick 的小包（压缩后最小 3 字节）。
- 玩家完全挂机时连接也不会进入“零包”状态：客户端每 50ms 仍有包，服务端也有实体/世界同步。

### 2. 实测形状（#7423 评论里的 26.3 抓包）

| 状态 | c2s | s2c |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 站着不动 | 21 包/s，89 B/s | 41 包/s，5.6 KB/s |
| 转视角 | 35 包/s，267 B/s | 42 包/s，6 KB/s |
| 跑动 | 43 包/s，697 B/s | 99 包/s，69 KB/s |
| 进服加载 | 43 包/s | 2.2 MB / 12 s |

- 20Hz 节拍很稳（中位间隔 50.0ms）；加载卡顿出现过 4.7s 完全没有上行。
- 压缩后最小 tick 包 3 字节；`xmc:pad` 帧 7/11 字节（通道名 3/7 字符），包数能对上，字节略多。
- 下行大流量天然是 1400 字节 TCP 段，所以“区块下载”式的大流量在链路上本来就长这样。

### 3. 和 TLS 的区别

- TLS 记录层由应用写入驱动：16KB 记录可以连续满速，也可以长时间零包，没有固定节拍。
- Xray 的 VLESS/TLS 就是“静默 ↔ 满速”两态，所以登录握手后接一条 bulk 流，形状上说得通。
- MC 反过来：空闲也在走节拍，忙时也是“小块为主 + 偶尔大块”。
- 当前 XMC 的 `paddings` 是有限时间线（预置含 Play join 尾巴），走完就切到 `packetStream`；后者按代理数据的写入节奏、每块最多 24KB 直接发。于是：空闲时没有 20Hz 节拍，忙时是满速大块——这就是“和真实 MC 区别还很大”的地方。

### 4. 所以需要的是常驻整形

- 要模拟 MC，需要贯穿整个连接的 50ms tick 调度：每个 tick 按配额吐数据，把真实数据切小，再用 dummy payload 补足到目标包数/字节分布（idle/walk/load 分档）。
- 这正是你说的 XHTTP packet-up 那种 pipe：常驻发送器按节奏从 pipe 取数据，而不是启动时跑一遍有限序列。
- 稳态模型因此是“每 tick、每方向独立决策”，`clients`/`servers` 作为每侧模板/分布是合适的；但登录阶段的有限序列仍是有序的。

### 5. 对 #7456 的调整

同意“拆开就不好表达连续两次 c2s / 先 s2c”。所以：

- `clients` / `servers` 只放真正按侧区分的字段：`hostname`（client）、`yggdrasil`（client 账号 / server 校验端点）；
- `paddings` 保留现在的有序时间线（带 `direction`），这次不拆；等稳态 pacing 落地，再以 `clients.pacing` / `servers.pacing` 的“每侧模板”形式加入。

这样既能区分客户端/服务端，也不丢顺序表达能力。我按这个改 #7456 可以吗？

comments.issue_title: TUN inbound: Half-close the app connection when the outbound is done, instead of waiting for `uplinkOnly`
comments.body:
I tested #7347 on `main` and with #7364 applied. For ordinary VMess and VLESS, the patch removes the extra client-side wait. With Mux, the application already receives `FIN` as soon as the logical stream ends.

When aborting a connection with unread incoming data, `main` sends `RST`. With #7347, `Interrupt` falls back to `TCPWriter.Close()`, so TUN sends `FIN` first and then `RST` when the connection is fully closed.

[RFC 9293, §3.6.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html#section-3.6.1) recommends sending `RST` when closing a connection discards unread data. I suggest keeping `Close()` for graceful `FIN` and handling `Interrupt` separately. For an abort with unread data, preserve the existing `RST` behavior without a preceding `FIN` and add a regression test for it.

comments.issue_title: TUN inbound: Support configurable Wintun adapter `guid` on Windows
comments.body:
Could you clarify the example in the README about several engines sharing a TUN? It could be read as saying they can use the same adapter at the same time. Wintun allows only one active session per adapter, so the second engine would fail at `StartSession`.

I’d describe the behavior directly. The `guid` setting is used when creating a new adapter. If a Wintun adapter with the same name already exists, Xray opens it and keeps its existing GUID.

One small simplification in `ParseGUID` would be to check `len(s) == 36` and then call `uuid.Parse`. For a string of that length, the parser already checks the hyphen positions and hex digits, so there’s no need to format the result back into a string for comparison.

If you have a chance to test with Wintun on Windows, I’d suggest creating an adapter with a configured GUID and checking the actual GUID reported by Windows. It would also be worth checking that reopening an existing adapter by name preserves its GUID.

comments.issue_title: Leave Team
comments.body:
I think AI-assisted code review is a promising direction, and I'd like to share an example from my own experience.

I collected the history of Xray developers' discussions going back to the early days of the project, extracted key architectural decisions and the reasoning behind them, and used that material to build specialized skills and AI agents for code analysis, review, and testing.

This approach has already produced useful results. Instead of analyzing only the current source code, the agents can take the project's history, previous design decisions, and developers' experience into account when evaluating changes and designing test scenarios.

In my experience, this significantly reduces meaningless AI-generated suggestions and makes the analysis much more relevant. Of course, there is still plenty of room for improvement, and I continue refining the system for my own workflow. But the direction has proven practical.

A small part of this work is publicly available in my [Xray Core DevKit](https://github.com/svlavr/xray-core-devkit). It is more of an example of the tools and workflow than a finished universal solution.

I think we could go further and create a **publicly available AI toolkit specifically for Xray-core**, at least for preliminary PR review.

Such a toolkit could include knowledge of the project's architecture, development conventions, historical design decisions, specialized review agents, and testing procedures based on accumulated experience.

**PR authors could install this toolkit locally and run their changes through it before submitting a PR.**

This could help identify unnecessary modifications, architectural inconsistencies, compatibility issues, and common mistakes before maintainers have to review them.

Naturally, this would not replace human review or real testing. The idea is to provide a preliminary filter on the contributor's side, reducing the number of low-quality PRs and saving maintainers' time rather than creating even more AI-generated review comments for them to read.

In my opinion, the real value of AI here is not simply asking another model to review the code. It is about giving AI access to the project's accumulated engineering knowledge, architectural reasoning, and development experience, then using that context to evaluate changes and validate them through meaningful tests.

With the right approach, AI could actually reduce the maintainers' workload instead of adding to it.

comments.issue_title: TUN inbound: Support configurable Wintun adapter `guid` on Windows
comments.body:
> Claude review comment:
> 
> There's a byte-order bug in `adapterGUID`: it fills `Data1`, `Data2` and `Data3` with `binary.LittleEndian`, but in a GUID's text form those three groups are the field values written most significant byte first. So the adapter gets a different GUID than the one configured:
> 
> * `"guid": "6ba7b810-9dad-11d1-80b4-00c04fd430c8"` creates the adapter as `{10B8A76B-AD9D-D111-80B4-00C04FD430C8}`
> * `"01020304-0506-0708-090a-0b0c0d0e0f10"` becomes `{04030201-0605-0807-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}`
> 
> You can see it by comparing `adapterGUID(...).String()` with `windows.GUIDFromString("{" + guid + "}")`.
> 
> Could you please switch those three fields to `binary.BigEndian`, and update `TestAdapterGUID` to expect `Data1: 0x01020304, Data2: 0x0506, Data3: 0x0708`? Ideally the test would also check that `guid.String() == "{01020304-0506-0708-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}"`. The MD5 fallback can stay as it is, since that GUID is never shown to anyone as text, so its byte order doesn't matter.

Thanks, you're right — fixed in the follow-up commit:
"Fix the byte order of a configured Wintun GUID".

The canonical 16 bytes keep the first three groups big-endian (that's how
`CLSIDFromString` reads them), and I was reading them with `binary.LittleEndian`,
so every group reached the adapter swapped: `01020304-0506-0708-…` landed as
`{04030201-0605-0807-…}`.

- `tun_windows.go`: `binary.BigEndian` for `Data1`/`Data2`/`Data3`; `Data4` unchanged.
- `guid_windows_test.go`: the old test asserted the swapped struct, which is why it
  passed. It now expects `Data1 0x01020304, Data2 0x0506, Data3 0x0708` and also
  compares against `windows.GUIDFromString("{01020304-0506-0708-090A-0B0C0D0E0F10}")`
  and `GUID.String()`, so it is checked against Windows' own parsing and formatting
  rather than against my own assumption a second time.

The MD5 fallback is left alone, as you noted: its hash bytes are taken as the
struct does, same as before, and that GUID is never rendered as text.
